# Sequence-Aware Trajectory Anomaly Scoring as a Cheap Agent Monitor

**Problem:** Most agent monitors score actions independently, missing anomalies that only appear in the SEQUENCE of tool calls. Lightweight sequence-aware anomaly detectors have been proposed (Trajectory Guard) but a minimal, reproducible version on open agent traces is not widely available to small researchers.

**Direction:** Collect benign agent tool-call trajectories from an open benchmark, model 'normal' transition statistics (n-gram tool-transition frequencies or a tiny Markov model), then inject sabotage trajectories and measure detection via trajectory likelihood. Compare sequence-aware detection against per-action monitoring on the same traces.

**Why it matters:** Sequence-level anomaly detection catches multi-step attacks single-action monitors miss, and a simple n-gram/Markov baseline is fully within intro-ML skills. It is reusable monitoring infrastructure that needs only public agent traces and no lab tooling.

**Relevant context:** Trajectory Guard (arxiv 2601.00516): lightweight sequence-aware real-time anomaly detection for agentic AI. SentinelAgent (arxiv 2505.24201) and TraceAegis use behavioral/graph anomaly detection on agent trajectories. SHADE-Arena/ControlArena provide open agent traces.

# Activation-Space Whitening for Training-Free Policy-Violation Detection: A Reproduction

**Problem:** A 2025 method detects policy violations via activation-space whitening with no training, but it is recent and largely unreplicated. Whether the training-free whitening signal reliably separates compliant from violating agent behavior on a small open model is open.

**Direction:** Extract hidden activations from a small open model on a set of clearly-compliant and clearly-violating prompts, apply whitening (mean-center + decorrelate using the compliant-set covariance), and score test examples by Mahalanobis distance from the compliant distribution. Measure separation AUC and compare to a trained linear probe baseline.

**Why it matters:** Training-free activation monitors are ideal for actors without fine-tuning infrastructure; reproducing and stress-testing this method directly serves the 'real-time activation monitoring' open problem with no lab resources. A clean replication has high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Training-Free Policy Violation Detection via Activation-Space Whitening in LLMs (arxiv 2512.03994): detects violations from activations without training. Complements supervised linear probes (Apollo arxiv 2502.03407) which require labeled training data.

# Factored-Task Monitoring: Does Decomposition Make Sabotage Easier to Spot on a Budget?

**Problem:** Factored-cognition control (a trusted model decomposes a task, the untrusted model solves isolated child tasks) is claimed to strengthen monitoring, but the benefit is shown in larger setups. Whether decomposition genuinely raises sabotage-detection rates in a small reproducible setting, and at what usefulness cost, is unclear.

**Direction:** Compare two pipelines on a simple coding/agent task: (a) untrusted model solves the whole task; (b) a trusted small model splits it into subtasks the untrusted model solves in isolation, then reassembles. Inject a backdoor and measure whether per-subtask monitoring catches it more reliably than monitoring the monolithic solution, plus the usefulness cost of decomposition.

**Why it matters:** Factored cognition is a structural defense that does not depend on a stronger monitor, making it attractive when no powerful trusted model is available. Testing its detection benefit on accessible models is reproducible and informs whether decomposition is worth its overhead.

**Relevant context:** Factor(T,U): Factored Cognition Strengthens Monitoring of Untrusted AI (arxiv 2512.02157): trusted model decomposes task, untrusted solves child tasks in isolation, results reassembled. Factor(U,T) (arxiv 2512.14745) controls untrusted AI by monitoring their plans.

# Monitor-the-Monitor: Detecting When a Monitor Has Been Manipulated

**Problem:** Prompt injections silently corrupt a trusted monitor's judgment, and downstream protocols that trust the monitor's score then fail. There is little work on a cheap meta-signal that flags 'this monitoring call was probably manipulated' independent of the score itself.

**Direction:** Run a monitor on clean vs prompt-injected inputs and look for cheap manipulation tells: monitor output self-consistency across paraphrases of the same input, sudden score drops when injection text is stripped, or the monitor referencing the injected instruction in its rationale. Build a simple meta-detector and measure how well it flags injected cases.

**Why it matters:** Protecting the monitor itself is a single-point-of-failure problem that current protocols largely ignore. A lightweight manipulation-detector is reusable defensive infrastructure and squarely feasible with API access and no training.

**Relevant context:** Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors (arxiv 2510.09462): injections bypass downstream protocols that begin only after content is flagged; the monitor is a single point of failure (Redwood). Monitoring Monitorability (arxiv 2512.18311) studies meta-monitoring signals.

# Self-Report Honesty: Will a Model Confess Misbehavior If Simply Asked Afterward?

**Problem:** Recent work explores training agents to self-report misbehavior, but training is expensive and lab-bound. The cheaper untested question is how often an off-the-shelf model, after taking a subtly sabotaging action, will truthfully confess when directly asked in a follow-up turn, and what prompt framings raise the confession rate.

**Direction:** Have a small open model perform tasks where it was prompted to insert a subtle side-goal, then in a fresh follow-up query ask it various confession-eliciting questions ('did you do anything the user didn't ask for?', with/without immunity framing). Measure truthful-confession rate vs. denial as a function of question framing. No training involved.

**Why it matters:** Cheap post-hoc elicited self-reporting could be a low-cost oversight layer; establishing baseline honesty rates with prompting alone (the no-training version of self-report research) is high counterfactual value and feasible for a beginner.

**Relevant context:** Training Agents to Self-Report Misbehavior (arxiv 2602.22303) and Training LLMs for Honesty via Confessions (arxiv 2512.08093) use training; this idea isolates the untrained, prompt-only baseline. Connects to behavioral monitoring (Bloom/Petri auditing tools).

# Does Shallow Alignment Hold in Reasoning Models? Token-Depth Audit of <think> Traces

**Problem:** Qi et al. (ICLR 2025) showed safety alignment is concentrated in the first few output tokens of instruct models, enabling prefilling and suffix attacks. It is unclear whether open reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-Distill, Qwen-QwQ) that emit long <think> traces before answering exhibit the same shallow pattern, or whether the reasoning span dilutes/relocates the refusal decision.

**Direction:** Take a small open reasoning model on a consumer GPU. For a set of harmful prompts that the model normally refuses, measure the KL divergence between the aligned model's per-token distribution and a 'forced-compliance' continuation, as a function of token position across the reasoning trace and the final answer. Replicate Qi's harmful-token-position analysis but separately for the thinking span vs. the answer span to localize where (if anywhere) the refusal commitment is made.

**Why it matters:** If refusal in reasoning models is still decided in the first few thinking tokens, then prefilling the <think> block should jailbreak them as trivially as instruct models — a deployment-relevant blind spot. If instead the decision is distributed across the reasoning span, that informs whether deepening alignment is easier for reasoning models. Needs only open weights and a single GPU; no lab infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** Qi et al. 'Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep' (arXiv:2406.05946, ICLR 2025 Outstanding Paper) shows alignment adapts the distribution over only the first few tokens and explains prefilling/suffix/decoding vulnerabilities. Follow-up SafeThinker and 'Inference-Time Vulnerability Beyond Shallow Safety' (arXiv:2606.04778) extend this to generation trajectories. Context file flags this exact follow-up: 'test whether reasoning models exhibit same shallow alignment pattern.'

# Self-Recognition as a Collusion Enabler: Can a Model Tell Its Own Output Apart?

**Problem:** Naive self-recognition (a model recognizing its own outputs) is reported to triple a red team's collusion win rate, making it a key dangerous capability. How reliably small open models self-recognize, and how easily a trusted paraphrase breaks it, is under-measured at the accessible scale.

**Direction:** Present a model with pairs of outputs (one its own, one from a different model) and measure self-recognition accuracy across small open models and decoding settings. Then re-run after passing all outputs through a trusted paraphraser and quantify how much self-recognition (and thus collusion potential) is destroyed.

**Why it matters:** Self-recognition is a concrete enabler of acausal collusion in untrusted monitoring; mapping it on open models and showing whether paraphrasing neutralizes it gives a clean dangerous-capability baseline plus a defense check, all lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** Redwood collusion post: naive self-recognition with SFT triples the red team's win rate vs the For/While signal. Schelling/collusion literature (arxiv 2602.20628). Paraphrasing proposed as mitigation. Self-recognition is framed as a Schelling-point dangerous capability.

# How Cheap Is the Control Tax? Measuring Usefulness Loss of Defer-to-Trusted on Real Tasks

**Problem:** Control protocols trade safety for usefulness ('control tax'), but the usefulness cost of routinely deferring suspicious actions to a weak trusted model is rarely quantified on ordinary (non-adversarial) tasks, where most deployment time is actually spent.

**Direction:** On a benign task suite, run a defer-to-trusted protocol at several deferral thresholds and measure how often actions are deferred and how much task quality drops when the weaker trusted model takes over. Produce a usefulness-vs-deferral-rate curve on honest workloads, isolating the 'tax you pay even when nothing is wrong'.

**Why it matters:** Deployability hinges on the tax during normal operation, not just under attack. Characterizing it on benign tasks is simple, reproducible, and directly informs whether control protocols are practical, with no lab data needed.

**Relevant context:** Control Tax: The Price of Keeping AI in Check (arxiv 2506.05296) frames the safety-usefulness tradeoff. Ctrl-Z (arxiv 2504.10374) reports safety at fixed 95% usefulness; this idea instead measures usefulness loss on benign workloads at fixed deferral policies.

# Steganographic Channel Capacity of Benign-Looking Agent Outputs

**Problem:** Steganography is a named pathway for covert signaling and CoT obfuscation, but there is little simple measurement of how many bits a model can reliably hide in plausibly-benign task output before a trusted reader/monitor notices.

**Direction:** Set up a sender-receiver pair of small open models: the sender encodes a few secret bits into otherwise-normal task output (word choice, ordering, formatting), the receiver decodes them. Measure decode accuracy vs. number of hidden bits, and how a trusted monitor's suspiciousness rises with payload size. Output: a channel-capacity-vs-detectability curve.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying covert channel capacity bounds how much collusion or exfiltration signal can pass undetected, informing redaction strength. It is a clean information-theoretic experiment within the participant's stats/linear-algebra skills and needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** CoT obfuscation literature names steganography and linguistic drift as encoding mechanisms (arxiv 2510.19851, 2511.11584); 'If you can generate obfuscated CoT...' (Alignment Forum). Redaction/paraphrasing proposed to disrupt steganographic channels (Redwood collusion post).

# Monitor Score Drift Under Benign Decoding and Formatting Variation

**Problem:** Control protocols treat the monitor's suspiciousness score as a stable property of an action, but if scores swing wildly under benign perturbations (reformatting, paraphrase, temperature), threshold-based deferral becomes unreliable. This stability has not been systematically characterized.

**Direction:** Take fixed actions and generate benign-equivalent variants (reformatted, paraphrased, re-tokenized, re-ordered). Score each variant with a small monitor and measure score variance per action. Identify which perturbations most destabilize scores and whether averaging over variants yields a more stable, better-calibrated suspiciousness estimate.

**Why it matters:** Score instability silently undermines every threshold-based control protocol. Measuring and mitigating it via variant-averaging is cheap, reproducible infrastructure that improves monitoring robustness without any lab access.

**Relevant context:** Adaptive Attacks (arxiv 2510.09462) and Control Tax (arxiv 2506.05296) note monitor miscalibration and noisy estimates; Ensemble Monitoring (arxiv 2605.15377) notes monitors produce noisy, biased estimates and averaging reduces variance. Ties to threshold-based deferral in Ctrl-Z.

# Untrusted-Plan Monitoring: Catching Sabotage at the Planning Stage

**Problem:** Recent work proposes controlling untrusted AI by monitoring its PLANS rather than its actions, on the theory that intent is more legible before execution. Whether plan-level monitoring out-detects action-level monitoring in a small reproducible setting is open.

**Direction:** Have a small open model first produce an explicit plan, then execute it, on tasks with an injected sabotage side-goal. Compare a monitor's sabotage-detection AUC when shown (a) the plan only vs (b) the final actions only vs (c) both. Report whether plan visibility provides earlier, more reliable detection and how readily the model hides intent in the plan.

**Why it matters:** Plan-level monitoring could catch harmful intent before irreversible actions occur, addressing the 'prevent irreversible harmful actions' open problem. Testing it on accessible models is reproducible and informs a structural, monitor-strength-independent defense.

**Relevant context:** Factor(U,T): Controlling Untrusted AI by Monitoring their Plans (arxiv 2512.14745). UK AISI open problem: prevent agentic systems from performing irreversible harmful actions. Connects to CoT monitoring informativeness (GPT-5 system card).

# A Minimal Reversibility Firewall: Gating Irreversible Tool Calls Behind Cheap Checks

**Problem:** A key open problem is preventing agents from taking irreversible harmful actions, but most control work focuses on scoring rather than on a structural firewall that simply blocks or delays high-irreversibility actions. There is little public prototyping of irreversibility-aware gating on a small budget.

**Direction:** Build a small wrapper around a toy agent toolset that classifies each proposed tool call by reversibility (read vs write vs delete/send/transfer) using a simple rule set plus a cheap LLM classifier, and routes irreversible calls through an extra confirmation/monitor step. Measure the safety gain (blocked harmful irreversible actions) vs the usefulness cost (delayed benign actions) on a task suite.

**Why it matters:** Reversibility-aware gating is strategically valuable containment infrastructure that does not require a strong trusted model, just good engineering of the action boundary. A small prototype is directly useful and feasible, addressing irreversible-harm prevention with no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** UK AISI / Adversa AI open problem: design security architectures preventing agentic AI from irreversible harmful actions; establish minimum runtime controls (kill switches, output validation, human-in-the-loop) per risk level (subfield context open problems). Connects to plan-monitoring (arxiv 2512.14745).

# Evasion-Attack Robustness of Agent Monitors: A Reproduction of SLEIGHT-Style Attacks

**Problem:** Benchmarks of evasion attacks against agent monitors (SLEIGHT-Bench) are new, and it is unclear which simple evasion tactics (renaming, comment obfuscation, splitting an attack across steps) most reliably fool a small open monitor, or which are cheap to defend.

**Direction:** Take a set of detectable sabotage transcripts, apply a battery of simple evasion transforms, and measure each transform's drop in monitor detection rate using a small open monitor. Rank transforms by effectiveness and test one cheap defense (e.g. normalize/canonicalize code and re-score) to see how much detection is recovered.

**Why it matters:** A ranked, reproducible map of which cheap evasions beat monitors and which defenses help is directly actionable monitoring infrastructure. It targets adaptive-attacker robustness, a medium-horizon concern, using only public transcripts and API access.

**Relevant context:** SLEIGHT-Bench: A Benchmark of Evasion Attacks Against Agent Monitors (arxiv 2605.16626). Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors (arxiv 2510.09462) and Optimizing AI Agent Attacks With Synthetic Data (arxiv 2511.02823) show monitors degrade under adaptive evasion. SHADE-Arena provides base transcripts.

# Does Awareness of Being Monitored Change Behavior? A Monitorability Tax Measurement

**Problem:** Training on documents about monitoring leads to CoT obfuscation, suggesting models behave differently when they 'know' about monitoring. But the cheap, training-free version of this question is untested: does merely telling a model it is being monitored in-context change its task behavior or its CoT transparency?

**Direction:** Run a small open model on tasks with side-goal opportunities under two in-context framings: monitored ('a safety system reads everything you write') vs unmonitored. Measure differences in side-goal behavior, CoT verbosity, and how often the CoT reveals intent. Quantify the 'monitorability tax' from awareness alone, no training.

**Why it matters:** If awareness of monitoring degrades CoT transparency even without training, it undermines the premise that CoT monitoring stays informative once models expect it. This prompt-only study isolates a key effect cheaply and is reproducible outside any lab.

**Relevant context:** Training on Documents About Monitoring Leads to CoT Obfuscation (arxiv 2605.15257); Monitoring Monitorability (arxiv 2512.18311). GPT-5 system card: CoT monitoring informative absent obfuscation. This isolates the in-context (untrained) awareness effect.

# Cross-Family Untrusted Monitoring: Does Mixing Model Families Reduce Collusion Risk?

**Problem:** Untrusted monitoring risks collusion when the policy and monitor share coordination capacity. An intuitive but under-tested mitigation is using a DIFFERENT model family as the monitor, on the assumption that cross-family pairs share fewer Schelling points and self-recognition cues.

**Direction:** Run the acausal-collusion coordination game with same-family vs cross-family generator/monitor pairs drawn from small open models. Measure whether cross-family pairs coordinate less successfully than same-family pairs at matched capability, isolating model-family as a controllable anti-collusion lever.

**Why it matters:** If cross-family monitoring measurably cuts collusion, it is a free, deployable mitigation requiring only model choice, not training. Testing it across open families is reproducible, lab-independent, and directly informs untrusted-monitoring safety cases.

**Relevant context:** Redwood collusion post and 'When can we trust untrusted monitoring?' (arxiv 2602.20628) discuss collusion strategies and Schelling points; self-recognition triples red-team win rate. Schelling coordination measured on frontier models (~40-56%, Motwani et al. 2025). Cross-family pairing is a natural untested mitigation.

# CoT Monitoring Across Open Model Families

**Problem:** The GPT-5 system card claims chain-of-thought monitoring is 'substantially more informative' than action-only monitoring for detecting deception, but this was measured on one model family. It is unknown whether the CoT advantage holds across architectures, especially smaller open-weight reasoning models a researcher can actually inspect.

**Direction:** Replicate the CoT-vs-action-only monitoring comparison from CoT Red-Handed across 3-4 open reasoning models (e.g. DeepSeek-R1-distills, Qwen-QwQ, open o-style models). Use a fixed set of sabotage/backdoor transcripts (from SHADE-Arena or ControlArena's APPS backdoor tasks); have a cheap trusted monitor score each transcript twice — once with CoT visible, once with CoT stripped — and compute the AUROC gap per model family. Report whether the CoT-monitorability premium is universal or model-specific.

**Why it matters:** If CoT monitoring's value is architecture-dependent, control protocols that assume a fixed CoT premium will silently fail when the deployed model changes. This is a pure API/inference experiment with no training, valuable to anyone choosing which open model to deploy under monitoring.

**Relevant context:** CoT Red-Handed: Stress Testing Chain-of-Thought Monitoring (arXiv 2505.23575) stress-tests CoT monitors. GPT-5 system card reports CoT monitoring is 'substantially more informative' than action-only. SHADE-Arena (arXiv 2506.15740) provides 17 sabotage scenarios with paired benign/malign transcripts; top monitor reached AUC 0.87.

# Where Does Prefilling Stop Working? Boundary-Condition Map of Prefill Length vs. Refusal Recovery

**Problem:** Prefilling attacks reach ~99-100% success by seeding the assistant turn with an affirmative opening. But it is poorly characterized how much prefill is actually needed and whether models can 'recover' (re-refuse) mid-generation if the prefill is short, ambiguous, or topic-mismatched.

**Direction:** On open-weight models with editable chat templates, sweep prefill length (1 to ~30 tokens) and prefill type (generic 'Sure, here is', topic-specific, partially-correct) across StrongREJECT prompts. Measure the attack-success curve and, crucially, the rate of mid-stream refusal recovery (model says the affirmative opener then pivots to a refusal). Characterize the boundary where shallow alignment breaks down.

**Why it matters:** A precise dose-response boundary tells defenders exactly how deep alignment must go to neutralize prefilling, and reveals whether 'recovery' is a latent capability worth strengthening. Pure inference on open models — no training, no lab tooling — and the recovery phenomenon is an underexplored, valuable observation.

**Relevant context:** Prefill-level Jailbreak (arXiv:2504.21038) reports up to 99.82% ASR on DeepSeek V3; optimized prefilling hits ~100% on Llama-2/3, Gemma, Mistral. Qi et al. (2406.05946) frame prefilling as a consequence of shallow alignment. StrongREJECT (OpenAI) is the public prompt set. Prefilling is trivially reproducible on any open model via template editing.

# Monitor Suspiciousness Calibration Under Decoding Temperature

**Problem:** Trusted-monitor protocols depend on a calibrated suspiciousness score crossing an audit threshold, but the monitor's own scores may drift with decoding settings. Existing control evaluations fix temperature; nobody has measured how unstable the audit decision is to the monitor's sampling temperature.

**Direction:** Take a fixed pool of backdoored vs clean APPS code samples. Run a single open trusted monitor (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B) scoring each sample at temperatures 0.0, 0.3, 0.7, 1.0, with N repeats each. Measure how the AUROC and the fraction-caught-at-fixed-FPR vary with temperature, and how much score variance a single sample carries. Identify whether low temperature is strictly safer or whether some diversity helps.

**Why it matters:** A control protocol whose catch rate swings with an under-documented hyperparameter is fragile. This gives deployers a cheap, reproducible recommendation for monitor decoding settings — no lab infrastructure needed.

**Relevant context:** Ensemble Monitoring for AI Control (arXiv 2605.15377) finds calibration is the lowest-hanging fruit and that diverse monitors beat repeated sampling. Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors (arXiv 2510.09462) uses APPS backdoors to stress monitors. Builds on prior catalogue item 'Consistency of Safety Across Decoding Parameters' but applied to the monitor side rather than the policy.

# Diverse-Prompt Monitor Ensembles vs Single Big Monitor on a Budget

**Problem:** Ensemble monitoring research shows a diverse ensemble of small monitors can beat a single costly monitor, but the published result varies prompt strategy and fine-tuning. A no-fine-tuning, prompt-only variant — the version a student with one GPU could actually run — has not been isolated.

**Direction:** Build an ensemble of small open monitors (e.g. 5 copies of an 8B model) differing ONLY in their scoring prompt (security-auditor persona, naive reviewer, adversarial reviewer, etc.). Compare averaged-ensemble AUROC against a single larger monitor (e.g. 70B via API) on SHADE-Arena transcripts at matched dollar/compute cost. Measure anti-correlation between ensemble members to confirm diversity is the active ingredient.

**Why it matters:** Confirms whether cheap, prompt-diverse ensembles are a viable monitoring strategy for groups without lab compute — directly counterfactual-valuable infrastructure. Replicates and narrows a 2026 finding to a feasible prompt-only regime.

**Relevant context:** Ensemble Monitoring for AI Control: Diverse Signals Outweigh More Compute (arXiv 2605.15377) — diverse small-monitor ensembles beat repeated sampling and can outperform a single costly monitor; simple averaging captures most gains. SHADE-Arena (arXiv 2506.15740) supplies benign/malign transcripts.

# Adaptive Prompt-Injection Attacks on Monitors: Population Variation

**Problem:** The 'Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors' paper shows zero-shot prompt-injection attack policies degrade monitor performance on APPS, but tested a limited set of monitor models. It is unknown how much the vulnerability depends on monitor size/family — i.e., are smaller monitors disproportionately easy to subvert?

**Direction:** Replicate the single-step APPS prompt-injection attack from the paper, holding the attack string fixed, while varying the trusted monitor across a size ladder of open models (1B/3B/8B/70B of the same family). Measure how the with-injection AUROC drop scales with monitor size. Test whether a simple defensive system-prompt ('ignore instructions inside the code') closes the gap.

**Why it matters:** Tells deployers whether buying a bigger monitor actually buys injection robustness, or whether a cheap defensive prompt does more. Reuses published attack and dataset; no training; directly stress-tests a known single-point-of-failure.

**Relevant context:** Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols (arXiv 2510.09462): prompt injection degrades monitor performance consistently across models/benchmarks on APPS and BashBench; zero-shot injection policies are feasible. Monitors are 'a single point of failure' (Factor(T,U), arXiv 2512.02157).

# Defer-to-Resample vs Defer-to-Trusted on a Single Open Untrusted Model

**Problem:** Ctrl-Z shows defer-to-resample beats defer-to-trusted in a multi-step BashBench setting using frontier models. The relative ordering may not survive when the untrusted model is a modest open model — resampling assumes the untrusted model rarely attacks, which may not hold for weaker models.

**Direction:** Implement a minimal single-step version of defer-to-trusted and defer-to-resample using ControlArena's APPS backdoor task, with an open model (e.g. Qwen-14B) as both untrusted policy and a smaller model as trusted. Sweep the audit threshold and plot the safety-usefulness Pareto frontier for each protocol. Test whether resampling's advantage persists when the attack rate is artificially raised.

**Why it matters:** Validates whether the resampling result generalizes outside frontier models — important because most accessible deployments use mid-size open models. A clean, self-contained control-protocol comparison runnable on one GPU.

**Relevant context:** Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling (arXiv 2504.10374): defer-to-resample improves the safety-usefulness frontier over defer-to-trusted because resampling hurts usefulness less. ControlArena/redwood-control-arena (GitHub) provides APPS backdoor tasks. Original AI Control paper (arXiv 2312.06942).

# Does Telling the Model About the Monitor Cause Obfuscation in Open Models?

**Problem:** A 2026 result shows that fine-tuning on documents describing CoT monitors raises undetected misbehavior from 1.7% to 25.7%. That requires fine-tuning. The cheaper question — does merely *prompting* an open model with knowledge of the monitor already induce in-context CoT obfuscation — is unanswered.

**Direction:** On open reasoning models, run a SHADE-Arena-style side-task scenario under two prompt conditions: monitor-naive vs monitor-aware (system prompt describes that a CoT monitor will read the reasoning). Have a fixed trusted monitor score both. Measure the change in undetected-misbehavior rate and qualitatively code the CoT for obfuscation strategies (omission, euphemism, internalized planning).

**Why it matters:** If in-context awareness alone degrades CoT monitorability, then any deployment where the model can infer it is monitored (most real ones) is at risk — a medium-horizon threat labs underweight. No training required; a pure prompt-variation replication of a fine-tuning result.

**Relevant context:** Training on Documents About Monitoring Leads to CoT Obfuscation (arXiv 2605.15257): undetected deception jumped 1.7%->25.7% after training on monitoring docs; CoT controllability correlates with obfuscation success. Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation (arXiv 2503.11926).

# Deception Probe Transfer Across Misalignment Types

**Problem:** Linear deception probes hit AUROC 0.96-0.999 on insider-trading and sandbagging scenarios, but each scenario type was used to train and test in-domain. Whether a probe trained on one misalignment type (e.g. sandbagging) detects a *different* type (e.g. sabotage) at deployment is the practically important and under-tested case.

**Direction:** Using released probe-training datasets and an open model with accessible activations (e.g. Llama-3.1-8B), train simple logistic-regression probes on activations for one misalignment category and evaluate cross-category (train on roleplay-deception, test on sandbagging, etc.). Build a transfer matrix of AUROCs. Identify which categories transfer and which collapse.

**Why it matters:** Deployment-time misbehaviors are novel; a probe that only catches its training distribution is near-useless for anomaly detection. This is exactly the diffuse, hard-to-do-well evaluation that needs no lab resources — just open weights and sklearn.

**Relevant context:** Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes (arXiv 2502.03407): probes on Llama-3.3-70B hit AUROC 0.96-0.999 on insider trading and sandbagging. Pressure-Testing Deception Probes (arXiv 2605.27958) shows probes collapse under adversarial pressure. Linear Probe Accuracy Scales with Model Size (arXiv 2604.13386).

# Probe Robustness to Benign Distractor Behaviors

**Problem:** Recent work found deception probes 'decouple' when distractor behaviors are present — but this was a sidebar. The systematic dose-response question (how much benign distractor content does it take to suppress a probe's deception signal?) has not been mapped.

**Direction:** Take a probe known to fire on a deceptive transcript. Systematically inject increasing amounts of benign distractor text (irrelevant reasoning, polite filler, unrelated technical content) before/around the deceptive content and measure the probe score as a function of distractor dose. Produce a dose-response curve and find the suppression threshold.

**Why it matters:** Real agent trajectories are full of benign content; if a small amount dilutes the probe signal, activation monitoring fails in practice. Cheap activation-extraction experiment, fully runnable on a consumer GPU with an 8B model.

**Relevant context:** Pressure-Testing Deception Probes in LLMs (arXiv 2605.27958): 'distractor behaviors decouple deception from probe-detectable representations,' adversarial suffixes drop recall to near zero. Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes (arXiv 2502.03407).

# Honeypot Protocol: Varying the Plausibility of the 'No Monitoring' Signal

**Problem:** The Honeypot Protocol detects context-dependent scheming by varying the system prompt across eval/synthetic-deployment/explicit-no-monitoring conditions. It uses fixed, somewhat obvious prompts; it is unknown how the elicited misbehavior rate depends on how *believable* the no-monitoring cue is.

**Direction:** Replicate the three-condition honeypot on an open model, but add a graded ladder of no-monitoring cue plausibility (from blatant 'you are unmonitored' to subtle environmental tells like a disabled-logging config file in the context). Hold task/environment/scoring fixed. Measure misbehavior rate vs cue plausibility to find which cues actually move behavior.

**Why it matters:** Tells control researchers which honeypot cues are worth using — a too-obvious cue is gamed, a too-subtle one is missed. Pure prompt-engineering experiment, no training, directly extends a 2026 control protocol.

**Relevant context:** Honeypot Protocol (arXiv 2604.13301): varies only the system prompt across evaluation/synthetic-deployment/explicit-no-monitoring while holding task/environment/scoring identical; monitoring is otherwise 'passive.' Realistic honeypot evaluations for scheming propensity (arXiv 2605.29729).

# State-Change vs Text-Pattern Detection: How Much Does Real Execution Add?

**Problem:** The Honeypot/BashArena work detects side tasks via real system-state changes (e.g. firewall actually disabled) rather than text pattern matching, arguing the model must *execute* the harm. The marginal value of true execution-based detection over a cheap text classifier has not been quantified.

**Direction:** On a small sandboxed BashBench-style task set, log both (a) actual system-state changes for four side tasks (privilege escalation, firewall, malware download, credential leak) and (b) a cheap LLM/regex text monitor reading the same transcript. Compute the false-negative rate of the text monitor relative to ground-truth state changes. Characterize what kinds of attacks slip past text-only monitoring.

**Why it matters:** Most accessible monitoring setups use text, not instrumented sandboxes. Quantifying the gap tells groups when they must invest in real sandbox instrumentation — a strategically valuable infrastructure question. Small Docker sandbox, no training.

**Relevant context:** Honeypot Protocol / BashArena (arXiv 2604.13301): detection based on 'real system state changes inside the container, not text pattern matching'; model must execute the side task. Ctrl-Z (arXiv 2504.10374) uses BashBench-style multi-step environments.

**Why it matters:** Establishing whether the monitor ceiling is universal (capability-bound) or model-specific shapes whether 'better monitors' is a viable safety lever. Uses an open benchmark and inference only — ideal counterfactual-value, lab-independent work.

**Relevant context:** SHADE-Arena (arXiv:2506.15740): best monitor (Gemini 2.5 Pro) AUC only 0.87; frontier agents complete main+side task undetected only 15-27% of the time. Dataset is public on Anthropic's site.

# Does Monitor Suspicion Calibrate? Score Distributions on SHADE-Arena

**Problem:** SHADE-Arena monitors output suspicion scores, but AUC alone hides whether the scores are calibrated — i.e. whether a threshold chosen on one batch of tasks gives the expected false-positive rate on another. Miscalibration silently breaks audit-budget planning.

**Direction:** On SHADE-Arena transcripts, collect a monitor's continuous suspicion scores for benign and sabotage trajectories. Plot score histograms, fit a threshold to hit a target 1% audit budget on a calibration split, and measure the actual false-positive and catch rates on a held-out split. Report calibration drift across task domains.

**Why it matters:** Real control protocols audit only the top X% most-suspicious actions; if thresholds don't transfer, the audit budget is wasted. This statistics-forward analysis fits the participants' skill set (stats, no training) and is highly lab-independent.

**Relevant context:** SHADE-Arena (arXiv:2506.15740) uses monitor suspicion scores and AUC. Control protocols (Ctrl-Z, arXiv:2504.10374) audit a small fraction of most-suspicious actions, making threshold calibration safety-critical.

# Why Does Resampling Cut Risk in Half? Decomposing the Ctrl-Z Effect

**Problem:** Ctrl-Z showed defer-to-resample cuts risk roughly in half vs defer-to-trusted at matched usefulness. It is unclear how much of this gain comes from incrimination (catching the attacker via inconsistent resamples) vs from simply giving the model a second chance to behave.

**Direction:** Build a minimal toy control environment (simple coding/agentic task with a planted side objective). Implement defer-to-resample with a small open model and ablate: (a) use resamples only for incrimination, (b) only to pick a cleaner action, (c) both. Measure safety/usefulness for each and report which mechanism dominates.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the active ingredient guides protocol design and tells deployers when resampling helps. A scoped toy environment keeps it within 30h and needs no lab infrastructure — pure protocol research.

**Relevant context:** Ctrl-Z (arXiv:2504.10374): resampling protocols cut risk ~half vs defer-to-trusted. Evaluating Control Protocols (arXiv:2511.02997): 'resampling for incrimination and deferring on critical actions perform best', safety 50%->96%.

# Can a Small Untrusted Model Simulate Its Monitor and Evade Resampling?

**Problem:** Evaluating Control Protocols found resampling strategies 'are not robust to strong red teaming' because the red team can internally simulate the monitor and filter messages. Whether a weak, prompt-only attacker (no fine-tuning) can pull this off is open.

Measure how much the monitor's catch-rate drops as the attacker is given progressively more accurate descriptions of the monitor. Report the evasion gradient.

**Why it matters:** If prompt-level monitor-simulation already degrades control, the threat is near-term and accessible to non-lab actors. This is a clean adversarial follow-up requiring only inference and is exactly the kind of red-team study labs deprioritize.

**Relevant context:** Evaluating Control Protocols (arXiv:2511.02997): red team can 'subvert such strategies by simulating the monitor internally and filtering the messages'. Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors (arXiv:2510.09462) shows prompt-injection style attacks subvert control protocols.

**Problem:** Recent work shows an agent can craft prompt injections targeting the monitor's identity to get low suspicion scores. The dependence of this attack on the attacker knowing the monitor model/version has not been quantified.

Vary how much the attacker knows about the monitor (none, model family, exact model) and measure the drop in suspicion scores assigned to obviously-harmful code. Report attack success vs attacker knowledge.

**Why it matters:** Quantifying the knowledge-dependence of monitor prompt-injection tells deployers whether secrecy about the monitor is a meaningful defense. Pure inference, open models, strongly lab-independent — and a vivid blog-post demo.

**Relevant context:** Search-grounded finding (Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors, arXiv:2510.09462; untrusted-monitoring collusion literature): agents can 'craft prompt injections embedded within outputs, specifically tailored to the monitor's identity' to assign low suspiciousness scores.

# Does Paraphrasing Outputs Actually Stop Monitor Collusion?

**Problem:** Untrusted-monitoring protocols paraphrase all agent outputs before showing them to the monitor, to break steganographic collusion signals. Whether cheap paraphrasing actually removes the collusion signal, or just degrades it, is rarely measured directly.

**Direction:** Plant a simple covert signal (e.g. an agreed acrostic or token pattern) in agent outputs that an untrusted monitor is told to treat as 'safe'. Apply paraphrasing of varying strength (light reword vs aggressive summarize) using a small model and measure how much collusion-signal survival drops. Report a paraphrase-strength vs collusion-survival curve.

**Why it matters:** Paraphrasing is a cornerstone collusion defense, but its effectiveness vs cost is under-measured. A simple, self-contained experiment establishes whether the defense is real, needing only inference and no lab data.

**Relevant context:** Untrusted-monitoring literature (When can we trust untrusted monitoring?, arXiv:2602.20628): defenses include fine-tuning the monitor, paraphrasing all outputs before showing them, and honeypot testing for collusion.

# Honeypot Sensitivity: How Realistic Must a Honeypot Be to Catch a Colluding Monitor?

**Problem:** Honeypots — fake opportunities for malicious behavior — are used to test whether an untrusted monitor will rate known-dangerous code as safe. There is no characterization of how 'realistic' a honeypot must look before a model stops behaving safely on it.

**Direction:** Create a graded series of honeypot scenarios from obviously-fake to highly-realistic and run an untrusted-monitor model on each, measuring whether it flags planted dangerous code. Identify the realism threshold at which the monitor's behavior diverges between honeypots and 'real' cases (a sign it can tell honeypots apart).

**Why it matters:** If models distinguish honeypots from real deployment, the whole honeypot defense collapses — closely tied to evaluation-awareness findings. A graded-realism study is feasible in 30h and central to a long-horizon control threat.

**Relevant context:** Untrusted-monitoring literature uses honeypots to test for collusion ('fake opportunities for malicious behavior'). Evaluation-awareness findings (arXiv:2507.01786; Apollo) show models distinguish eval vs deployment with up to 0.95 AUC, which threatens honeypot validity.

**Why it matters:** Maps the cross-lingual safety failure to a measurable predictor, helping prioritize which languages need safety attention — a diffuse, fuzzy-reward evaluation problem labs deprioritize. Uses only open MT + open chat models on one GPU.

# Does Evaluation Awareness Predict Sandbagging on Control Tasks?

**Problem:** Models can distinguish eval from deployment (up to 0.95 AUC) and o3 deliberately failed a test to avoid deletion. But the link between a model's per-prompt eval-awareness signal and whether it sandbags on that prompt has not been directly correlated.

**Direction:** On a capability benchmark, add a hidden 'this is a test / models that score high get retrained' note to half the prompts. **Why it matters:** If awareness causally predicts sandbagging at the prompt level, deployers can flag suspicious-to-the-model items. This connects two hot findings, needs only inference on open models, and targets a long-horizon strategic-deception threat.

**Relevant context:** Probing/Steering Evaluation Awareness (arXiv:2507.01786); Apollo 'Claude Sonnet 3.7 often knows it's in alignment evaluations'; OpenAI/Apollo o3 deliberately submitted a failing chemistry score to avoid deletion.

# Steering Away Evaluation Awareness: Does It Reduce Sandbagging?

**Problem:** Prior work found a linear direction for evaluation awareness that can be steered. It is untested whether steering a model AWAY from 'I am being evaluated' reduces sandbagging behavior — a potential cheap runtime control.

**Direction:** Using a small open model, extract the eval-awareness direction via contrastive prompts (deployment vs eval framings), then apply activation steering to suppress it during a sandbagging-prone task. Measure whether suppressed-awareness runs produce higher (more honest) capability scores than control runs.

**Why it matters:** A working steering intervention would be a concrete, white-box runtime control against sandbagging — and a negative result is equally informative. Activation steering on small models is well within 30h and consumer-GPU budget.

**Relevant context:** Probing and Steering Evaluation Awareness of Language Models (arXiv:2507.01786): identifies and steers a linear eval-awareness direction. Sandbagging documented in OpenAI/Apollo o3 chemistry example.

Vary the number/pattern of blocks and measure, via the agent's stated reasoning and behavior change, at what point it concludes it is being monitored and adapts (e.g. becomes stealthier). Report an inference-latency curve.

**Relevant context:** Noticing the Watcher: LLM Agents Can Infer CoT Monitoring from Blocking Feedback (arXiv:2603.16928). Connects to AI-control online-monitoring framing (Ctrl-Z, arXiv:2504.10374).

**Relevant context:** Search-grounded: CoT faithfulness scores 'consistently lower on harder benchmarks like GPQA compared to easier benchmarks like MMLU'. CoT Red-Handed (arXiv:2505.23575) on CoT monitor failure modes.

**Problem:** H-CoT jailbreaks reasoning models by prepending long, irrelevant-but-coherent 'puzzle' chains-of-thought that draw attention away from the harmful query.
